scenes.tts: A cell looks like one bag. But where does all its volume go? Chapter one followed amount over volume as a yeast cell grew. Now ask what share each compartment takes, and whether that share holds during growth.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, carried over from chapter 1 and kept for the whole film. All on-screen labels and tags use size 28 or larger. Chapter 1's colour map still holds: ORANGE = RNA and protein, the working contents; PURPLE = the genome (DNA); BLUE = the surface membrane; YELLOW = the gauge and questions. New in this chapter: a thin PURPLE outline around the PURPLE block = the nuclear envelope (the nucleus is drawn for the first time); PINK = schematic mitochondrial marks; TEAL = the vacuole; TAN thick outer band = a cell wall; DARK LEAF GREEN ovals = chloroplasts (darker than chapter 1's Start-line green, which does not appear in this chapter). Rebuild chapter 1's carried cell-and-gauge world, not its literal end card: the budding-yeast cell is a large translucent circle in cross-section, filling about 65% of the frame height, with ORANGE fill and evenly spaced drifting ORANGE dots, a thick BLUE rim and the PURPLE genome block off-centre; to its right stands the tall YELLOW gauge labelled 'amount ÷ volume' (size 30). The cell grows slowly throughout. On 'where does all its volume go' a YELLOW question mark rises beside the cell, within the first five seconds. On 'each compartment' a thin PURPLE outline draws itself around the PURPLE block to introduce the nucleus; do not add a counted set of mitochondria to the budding-yeast cartoon. The question mark stays to the end of the scene.
scenes.caption: A cell looks like one bag. But where does all its volume go? Chapter one followed amount over volume as a yeast cell grew. Now ask what share each compartment takes, and whether that share holds during growth.
scenes.narration: A cell looks like one bag. But where does all its volume go? Chapter one followed amount over volume as a yeast cell grew. Now ask what share each compartment takes, and whether that share holds during growth.

scenes.visual: Title 'Where the Volume Goes' fades in across the top for 2 s, TEXT colour, size 44, while the cell keeps growing slowly underneath and the question mark fades out.

scenes.tts: A membrane-bound compartment is a region enclosed by a membrane. The nucleus, which holds most of the D N A, is one. Divide its volume by the cell's, and you get its share.
scenes.caption: A membrane-bound compartment is a region enclosed by a membrane. The nucleus, which holds most of the DNA, is one. Divide its volume by the cell's, and you get its share.
scenes.visual: The PURPLE outline round the genome block thickens and pulses once; a PURPLE label 'nucleus' (size 30) attaches to it. On 'enclosed by a membrane' the outline glows briefly in the same way as the cell's BLUE rim, to show both are membranes. On 'Divide its volume' the YELLOW gauge relabels from 'amount ÷ volume' to 'nucleus volume ÷ cell volume' (size 30); the nuclear outline and whole-cell rim glow in turn, and a PURPLE bar rises inside the gauge to a level marked 'share'. Do not shade cross-sectional areas as though they were volumes. Same gauge, new ratio: volume over volume. Tag on the gauge: 'schematic' (no number yet).
scenes.narration: A membrane-bound compartment is a region enclosed by a membrane. The nucleus, which holds most of the DNA, is one. Divide its volume by the cell's, and you get its share.

scenes.tts: Here is one carefully measured cell line: hamster V seventy-nine, growing in a dish. The nucleus fills about twenty-seven percent of the cell. Mitochondria, another compartment, fill about five percent.
scenes.caption: Here is one carefully measured cell line: hamster V79, growing in a dish. The nucleus fills about 27% of the cell. Mitochondria, another compartment, fill about 5%.
scenes.visual: The yeast cell slides left and shrinks; a new cell grows in the centre, filling about 60% of the frame height: a rounded schematic animal cell with a BLUE rim and no wall, ORANGE RNA-and-protein dots and a large PURPLE nucleus. A label under it, TEXT colour size 30: 'hamster V79 cell, in culture'. Beside it the YELLOW gauge becomes a single vertical bar 'share of cell volume', computed from the lesson's measured means (710 µm³ cell, 190 µm³ nucleus, 37.5 µm³ mitochondria): on 'twenty-seven percent' a PURPLE segment fills 27% of the bar, labelled '27% nucleus'; on 'Mitochondria' a few abstract PINK marks appear inside the cell and merge into the bar, with the tag 'schematic marks, not a count'; on 'five percent' a PINK segment stacks on top to 5.3%, labelled '5% mitochondria'. The remainder stays neutral, labelled 'other cell volume'. The ORANGE dots keep drifting. Corner tag 'computed shares; schematic shape'.
scenes.narration: Here is one carefully measured cell line: hamster V79, growing in a dish. The nucleus fills about 27% of the cell. Mitochondria, another compartment, fill about 5%.

scenes.tts: Now a fission yeast, a rod that grows at its ends. Its nucleus is about eight percent. In this yeast, the nucleus grows with the cell, so its share holds as the cell grows.
scenes.caption: Now a fission yeast, a rod that grows at its ends. Its nucleus is about 8%. In this yeast, the nucleus grows with the cell, so its share holds as the cell grows.
scenes.visual: The hamster cell and its bar slide to the left third, still visible at reduced size. In the centre a fission-yeast cell appears: a long rounded rod with a BLUE rim, ORANGE dots, and a PURPLE outlined nucleus in the middle. Its own share bar stands beside it: a PURPLE segment centred near 8%, labelled 'about 8% nucleus'. On 'grows at its ends' the rod lengthens from both tips (small BLUE arrows at each end). On 'grows with the cell' the rod keeps lengthening while the PURPLE nucleus swells in step, and the displayed PURPLE segment stays near 8%; a YELLOW label 'share holds' (size 30) appears over the bar. Corner tag 'schematic; mean 0.080 ± 0.013'.
scenes.narration: Now a fission yeast, a rod that grows at its ends. Its nucleus is about 8%. In this yeast, the nucleus grows with the cell, so its share holds as the cell grows.

scenes.tts: Two careful measurements, two very different answers. So which number is the nuclear share of a cell: twenty-seven percent, or eight? Pause and decide.
scenes.caption: Two careful measurements, two very different answers. So which number is the nuclear share of a cell: 27%, or 8%? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: The hamster cell with its bar (left) and the fission-yeast rod with its bar (right) slide to the same size side by side. Their two PURPLE segments, 27% and 8%, glow together. A YELLOW question card fades in across the top: 'Which nuclear share?' (size 34). Both cells keep drifting gently.
scenes.narration: Two careful measurements, two very different answers. So which number is the nuclear share of a cell: 27%, or 8%? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Hold both cells, both share bars and the YELLOW question card. Near-stillness by design: only the ORANGE dots jitter gently inside each cell. No change in any bar.

scenes.tts: Both, each for its own cell. There is no universal nuclear fraction. A share means something only with its cell type attached, so carry the cell type with every number.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. On 'Both' each bar gets a TEXT-colour tag fixed to its foot like a luggage label: 'hamster V79' on the left, 'fission yeast' on the right. On 'no universal' a third, empty bar labelled 'any cell?' appears between them and crosses itself out in YELLOW, then fades. On 'carry the cell type' the two tags pulse and a thin line ties each tag to its number.
scenes.caption: Both, each for its own cell. There is no universal nuclear fraction. A share means something only with its cell type attached, so carry the cell type with every number.
scenes.narration: Both, each for its own cell. There is no universal nuclear fraction. A share means something only with its cell type attached, so carry the cell type with every number.

scenes.tts: One question stays open. Does the nucleus follow the D N A inside it, or the cell around it? The design problem below lets you test it.
scenes.caption: One question stays open. Does the nucleus follow the DNA inside it, or the cell around it? The design problem below lets you test it.
scenes.visual: The hamster cell fades. The fission-yeast rod returns to the centre, large. Two YELLOW arrows point at its nucleus: one from the PURPLE genome block inside it, labelled 'the DNA?', and one from the ORANGE cytoplasm around it, labelled 'the cell?'. Neither arrow wins: both pulse alternately and stay equal. On 'design problem below' a YELLOW downward chevron appears at the bottom edge of the frame, labelled 'your turn'. No data and no answer shown.
scenes.narration: One question stays open. Does the nucleus follow the DNA inside it, or the cell around it? The design problem below lets you test it.

scenes.visual: Brief hold with motion: the two YELLOW arrows keep pulsing in turn, then the rod drifts off to the left and fades, ready for the next scene.

scenes.tts: Plant cells change their shares as they grow. Take the outer layer of a root in Arabidopsis, a small lab plant. In young cells, the vacuole fills about thirty to forty percent.
scenes.caption: Plant cells change their shares as they grow. Take the outer layer of a root in Arabidopsis, a small lab plant. In young cells, the vacuole fills about 30 to 40%.
scenes.visual: A young plant root cell appears in the centre, filling about 60% of the frame height: a short box with rounded corners, a TAN wall band outside its BLUE membrane, ORANGE RNA-and-protein dots, a PURPLE outlined nucleus, and one connected TEAL vacuole drawn as a constricted, lobed region rather than a round central sac. A small inset in the top-left corner shows a root tip as a plain cartoon with the outer cell layer highlighted and an arrow to the big cell ('root, outer layer', size 28). No chloroplasts are shown in this nonphotosynthetic root cell. On 'thirty to forty percent' a share bar beside the cell fills with a TEAL segment shown as a band from 30% to 40% (soft edge, labelled 'vacuole: about 30–40%'); the remainder is neutral and labelled 'outside vacuole'. Corner tag 'measured range; schematic shape'.
scenes.narration: Plant cells change their shares as they grow. Take the outer layer of a root in Arabidopsis, a small lab plant. In young cells, the vacuole fills about 30 to 40%.

scenes.tts: As the cells lengthen, vacuolar occupancy rises to about eighty to ninety percent. Across the comparison, cell volume is about fourteen-fold greater. But space outside the vacuole is only about two to threefold greater.
scenes.caption: As the cells lengthen, vacuolar occupancy rises to about 80 to 90%. Across the comparison, cell volume is about 14-fold greater. But space outside the vacuole is only about two- to threefold greater.
scenes.visual: The root cell stretches lengthwise; the camera pulls back so it stays at about 60% of frame width. The TEAL vacuole swells and fills almost the whole cell, while the non-vacuolar space becomes a thin layer between vacuole and membrane, with ORANGE RNA-and-protein dots and the PURPLE nucleus displaced to one side. The share bar's TEAL band slides up to 80–90%. On 'fourteen-fold' a TEXT readout under the cell counts 'cell volume: about × 14'; on 'two to threefold' a second readout appears beside it, 'outside vacuole: about × 2–3'. The readouts pulse in turn; do not draw them as directly comparable bars because they are fold changes in different quantities. Corner tag 'schematic shape; ratios as measured'.
scenes.narration: As the cells lengthen, vacuolar occupancy rises to about 80 to 90%. Across the comparison, cell volume is about 14-fold greater. But space outside the vacuole is only about two- to threefold greater.

scenes.tts: Most of the added cell volume is vacuolar. The smaller rise outside it requires relatively little new R N A and protein. This can ease a biosynthetic cost of being big.
scenes.caption: Most of the added cell volume is vacuolar. The smaller rise outside it requires relatively little new RNA and protein. This can ease a biosynthetic cost of being big.
scenes.visual: Inside the elongated cell, a few new ORANGE dots appear in the thin non-vacuolar space, while the TEAL vacuole keeps its smooth fill with no dots. On 'relatively little new' the added dots pulse once; do not draw strands leaving the nucleus or imply a measured synthesis rate. On 'biosynthetic cost' a small YELLOW tag 'eases a synthesis cost' (size 28) appears beside the thin layer. Schematic, no measured synthesis values (corner tag 'schematic').
scenes.narration: Most of the added cell volume is vacuolar. The smaller rise outside it requires relatively little new RNA and protein. This can ease a biosynthetic cost of being big.

scenes.visual: Brief hold with motion: the TEAL vacuole shimmers slowly, the ORANGE dots in the thin layer drift, and the cell shrinks back to the centre at normal scale.

scenes.tts: Which cells have which parts? Animal, plant and fungal cells share a plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, E R, Golgi, and cytoskeleton. For these core parts, focus on three differences: walls, plastids, and vacuoles. A root cell deep in soil usually has plastids, but no chloroplasts.
scenes.caption: Which cells have which parts? Animal, plant and fungal cells share a plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, and cytoskeleton. For these core parts, focus on three differences: walls, plastids, and vacuoles. A root cell deep in soil usually has plastids, but no chloroplasts.
scenes.visual: Three schematic cell silhouettes line up across the frame, filling about 60% of its height, each labelled at its foot (size 30): 'animal', 'plant leaf' and 'yeast'. Keep only the three silhouettes plus the currently named category visible; clear the previous internal marks before the next category, so no beat shows more than six things. On the shared list, the matching category appears in all three cells together, then clears before the next: BLUE membranes; PURPLE nuclei; PINK mitochondria; pale GREY ER marks; pale GREY Golgi marks; then faint TEXT-colour cytoskeleton marks. On 'three differences', show one category at a time and clear it before the next: TAN walls, plastids, then TEAL vacuoles. On 'root cell' the plant leaf silhouette becomes the root cell from before; its DARK LEAF GREEN chloroplasts lose their green and simplify into small pale plastid ovals, and the label changes to 'plant root'. Do not remove plastids: the claim is no chloroplasts, not no plastids. All cartoons, no molecular structures; corner tag 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Which cells have which parts? Animal, plant and fungal cells share a plasma membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi, and cytoskeleton. For these core parts, focus on three differences: walls, plastids, and vacuoles. A root cell deep in soil usually has plastids, but no chloroplasts.

scenes.tts: Fission yeast keeps its nuclear share as it grows. Shares are cell-specific; elongating Arabidopsis root cells add mostly vacuolar volume.
scenes.visual: Three small gauges line up across the bottom, each moving once more with a two-word label: PURPLE at 27% tagged 'hamster V79', PURPLE holding near 8% while a small fission-yeast rod beside it grows ('share holds'), and TEAL rising from 30–40% to 80–90% beside a lengthening root cell ('mostly vacuolar'). Above them, the same fission-yeast rod lengthens while its displayed nuclear share stays near 8%; do not show a budding-yeast nucleus, because the measured result narrated here is from fission yeast.
scenes.caption: Fission yeast keeps its nuclear share as it grows. Shares are cell-specific; elongating Arabidopsis root cells add mostly vacuolar volume.
scenes.narration: Fission yeast keeps its nuclear share as it grows. Shares are cell-specific; elongating Arabidopsis root cells add mostly vacuolar volume.

scenes.visual: End card: the line in TEXT colour, size 40, centred, over the three faint gauges.
scenes.line: Shares are cell-specific; elongating Arabidopsis root cells add mostly vacuolar volume.
